passage: "Jyoti, sit down, you're answering emails at dinner again. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty-four, I joined a big consulting firm. I was so proud. I answered every message at midnight, worked Sundays, skipped my cousin's wedding for a presentation. After a year I was tired all the time, snapping at my mother, crying in the office bathroom. One day my senior, a quiet man, said, 'Rehana, they'll take everything you give. Decide what you won't.' So I decided: no emails after nine, Sundays were mine, and I told my team so. I was scared they'd think I was lazy. Instead, my work got better. Beta, you'll have a long career. Don't burn it all in the first year."

qa.q: What did Rehana's senior say?
qa.a: 'They'll take everything you give. Decide what you won't.'

qa.q: How was Rehana feeling after the first year at the firm?
qa.a: Rehana was exhausted and stretched thin, snapping at Rehana's mother and crying in the office bathroom.

qa.q: What boundaries could Jyoti set, based on Rehana's story?
qa.a: Jyoti could stop checking emails after a set hour and keep one day a week free, telling the team so.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel hearing this at the dinner table?
qa.a: Jyoti might feel a bit caught out, but also relieved that someone older understands the pressure of a first job. 🙂

grounding: An elder tells a young worker how they set boundaries to recover from early burnout.

passage: It was his sister Mahima's birthday, and Jagdish, twenty-four, had promised to be home by seven. At five, his team lead messaged: a client wanted changes to the report by tomorrow morning. The office was emptying. His phone buzzed with a photo of the cake. Jagdish felt the old reflex: stay late, say yes, prove himself. Then he opened the report. Most of the changes were small. He estimated two hours. He messaged his lead: "I'll finish the main edits by 6:30 and the rest by 9 a.m. tomorrow. Is that okay?" The reply came: "Fine." He worked fast, logged off at 6:30 and caught the bus. At home, Mahima was blowing out candles when he walked in. She threw a cushion at him. "You came!"

qa.q: What time had Jagdish promised to be home?
qa.a: By seven.

qa.q: What did Jagdish feel pulled to do when the client's request came, and why?
qa.a: He felt pressured by the old urge to stay late and say yes to prove himself, even at the cost of his promise.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish's message to his lead a good way to set a boundary?
qa.a: It offered a clear, realistic plan that met the client's needs without giving up his evening, so both sides were respected.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt if he hadn't come?
qa.a: She'd likely have been hurt and disappointed, since it was her birthday and he had promised.

grounding: Shows a young professional under time pressure setting a work boundary to keep a family commitment.

passage: For the first three months at her job in Pune, Jahnavi, twenty-three, kept her work phone on her pillow. Every ping at night made her jump. Her roommate Jaya noticed she'd stopped going for their evening walks and ate dinner standing up. One Sunday, Jahnavi missed a college friend's call because she was fixing a slide nobody had asked for urgently. That night she sat on the balcony and felt tired all the way into her bones. On Monday, she turned off work notifications after eight and told her manager she'd reply to non-urgent messages in the morning. He said, "Of course." That was it. That evening she walked with Jaya past the lit-up food stalls, laughing about their college hostel. The phone stayed in her bag.

qa.q: After what time did Jahnavi turn off work notifications?
qa.a: After eight.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on the balcony on Sunday night?
qa.a: She felt deeply tired and worn out, realising how much of her life work had taken over.

qa.q: What small step helped Jahnavi most, and why?
qa.a: Turning off notifications after eight and telling her manager, because it protected her evenings without hurting her work.

qa.q: How might Jaya see the change in her roommate?
qa.a: Jaya would likely feel relieved to have a friend back for walks and conversation.

grounding: Shows a young professional in a city setting boundaries to prevent burnout in her first job.

passage:
"You're still on the laptop?" Nazia stood in the doorway with two cups of chai. "It's eleven, Indu."

"Just one more slide. My lead replied at ten, so…"

"So you have to reply at eleven?"

Indu rubbed her eyes. "In college I did this every night. It was fine."

"In college you slept till noon on Sundays. Now you're up at seven every day."

Indu laughed, then stopped. "My head's been hurting all week."

Nazia set the chai down. "What if you tell your lead you'll check messages till eight and after that it's morning?"

"What if she thinks I'm lazy?"

"Then she'll see your work at nine a.m. and think again."

Indu looked at the half-done slide, saved it, and closed the lid. "Okay. Eight. I'll tell her tomorrow." She took the chai. "Thanks, jaan."

qa.q: What time was it when Nazia brought the chai?
qa.a: It was eleven at night, according to Nazia.

qa.q: What was Indu afraid of when Nazia suggested a cut-off time?
qa.a: She was afraid her lead would think she was lazy if she stopped replying at night.

qa.q: What small step helped Indu, and what could she add next?
qa.a: Deciding on a clear eight o'clock cut-off and telling her lead helped; next she could keep the laptop out of her room so the rule is easier to keep.

qa.q: How does Nazia seem to see Indu's late nights?
qa.a: Nazia sees them as a college habit that no longer fits Indu's new life, and she seems worried about her friend's headaches and tiredness.

grounding: A dialogue shows a new worker setting a work boundary after noticing strain from carrying student-style habits into a job.

passage:
The first year at the architecture firm, I treated every deadline like a college jury. All-nighters, cold coffee, drawings emailed at 3 a.m. I was proud of it, honestly. I thought that was what serious people did.

By March I was snapping at my mother on the phone and forgetting simple dimensions. One evening Vasudha, the senior designer, found me redrawing a staircase for the fourth time. She didn't lecture. She just said, "Shreya, the site doesn't open until Monday. Go home."

That weekend I did something small. I wrote my own closing time on a card, seven-thirty, and taped it under my monitor. Some weeks I break it. But now when I stay late, I choose to, and my drawings have fewer mistakes. I still miss the adrenaline sometimes, which surprised me.

qa.q: What time did Shreya write on the card under her monitor?
qa.a: She wrote seven-thirty as her own closing time.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about her all-nighters at first, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt proud of them and saw them as what serious people do; later, after snapping at her mother and making mistakes, she realised they were wearing her down.

qa.q: What went well in how Vasudha helped Shreya?
qa.a: Vasudha gave a simple fact and a clear nudge to go home instead of a lecture, which let Shreya make her own decision about limits.

qa.q: How might Shreya's mother have experienced the change?
qa.a: She likely noticed Shreya was less irritable on calls once Shreya started leaving work at a set time.

grounding: A reflective account of a young architect moving from student all-nighters to a chosen daily limit to avoid burnout.

passage:
Coach's note, Lakeside Community Pool. Lavanya, adult squad.
Hafsa swam with our Tuesday–Thursday–Saturday group all through her final year at college. Strong, steady, never missed. After she started her first job in July, she came twice in six weeks, both times late, still in office clothes, answering her phone at the poolside.
In the third week of August I saw her sit on the bench with her cap in her hand and not get in. She said she was too tired to swim, then laughed as if it were a joke.
I asked if she wanted a lighter plan. We agreed on Saturday mornings only, phone in the locker, no exceptions.
She has come four Saturdays in a row now. Last week she told me she'd started logging off at seven on weekdays. Next step: I've asked her to help me with the beginners' lane once a month.

qa.q: What did Hafsa and the coach agree on?
qa.a: They agreed on Saturday mornings only, phone in the locker, no exceptions.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's laugh on the bench suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was more exhausted and worn down than she wanted to admit, hiding it behind a joke.

qa.q: Why was a lighter plan better than pushing Hafsa to return to three days?
qa.a: It gave her one protected slot she could actually keep, which helped her start setting other limits like logging off at seven.

qa.q: What would change if the coach had only scolded Hafsa for missing sessions?
qa.a: Hafsa might have felt ashamed and stayed away completely, instead of finding a routine that fit her new job.

grounding: A swimming coach notices a young graduate's routine collapse in her first job and helps her set a boundary.

passage:
Wednesday, 10:40 p.m.
Did it. Turned off work notifications at eight tonight. First time since I joined in April.
I was nervous all evening. Kept picking up the phone and putting it down. At nine I made proper dal instead of eating chips over the laptop. At 9:30 I called Amma and actually listened instead of saying “hmm” while typing.
At 10 Pallavi texted on my personal number: sorry, did you see the deck changes? I wrote back: I'll look first thing tomorrow 🙂 and then I felt guilty for ten whole minutes.
But college never had an end time, and this job doesn't either unless I give it one. Nothing broke tonight. The deck will still be there at nine.
Tomorrow I'll tell Pallavi my new hours, nicely. Going to bed before midnight. Imagine. — Shalini

qa.a: Shalini turned them off at eight.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling after replying to Pallavi?
qa.a: Shalini felt guilty for ten minutes after replying that the deck would wait, but also relieved that nothing broke.

qa.q: What could make Shalini's new boundary easier to keep?
qa.a: Telling Pallavi the new hours kindly, as planned, so colleagues know when to expect a reply.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Shalini's reply at 10 p.m.?
qa.a: Pallavi may accept it easily, since the message was friendly and gave a clear time to look at the deck.

passage: Manoj, twenty-four, taught maths at the government school in Sangamner. In his first term, he graded till midnight, answered parents' calls at dinner and spent Sundays making worksheets. By October, he was snapping at his own mother and couldn't remember the last time he'd played cricket. His colleague Jasleen, a teacher for eight years, found him asleep over a pile of notebooks in the staff room. "You won't last like this," she said. "I didn't either, my first year." She showed him how she worked: grading in school hours only, a fixed hour for parents' calls, Sundays off. Manoj tried it. The worksheets got simpler. The parents adjusted. On the second Sunday, he played cricket until sunset and came home laughing.

qa.q: What did Manoj spend his Sundays doing in his first term?
qa.a: Making worksheets.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel by October?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and irritable, snapping at his mother.

qa.q: What boundaries did Jasleen suggest?
qa.a: Grading only in school hours, a fixed hour for parents' calls and keeping Sundays off.

qa.q: How might Manoj's mother feel about the change?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and happy to have her cheerful son back.

passage: In their Johannesburg flat, Xin found Lindiwe, twenty-four, answering work emails on the sofa at 11 p.m. again. It was her third month as a junior accountant, and her phone buzzed through dinner, through films, even at 6 a.m. "You're not a doctor on call," Xin said. Lindiwe laughed, but her eyes were tired. "If I don't answer, they'll think I'm lazy." "Did anyone say that?" Lindiwe paused. "No." The next morning, she asked her manager directly. He looked surprised. "No one expects replies after seven." That night, Lindiwe switched off work notifications at seven. She felt twitchy for three days. By the second week, she was reading novels again and sleeping through the night.

qa.q: At what time did Lindiwe start switching off work notifications?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when she said "they'll think I'm lazy"?

qa.q: What step helped Lindiwe set a boundary?

passage: In the Pune IT office, Hemant, twenty-five, was always the last to leave. He thought staying late showed commitment. After six months, his back hurt, he'd stopped going to the gym, and his girlfriend had stopped asking about weekends. One evening, his team lead, Ayesha, stopped at his desk at eight. "Why are you still here?" "Finishing the report." "It's due Thursday. It's Monday." Hemant didn't answer. Ayesha sat down. "I burned out in my second year. Took me months to recover. Leave at six-thirty this week. Try it." He did, feeling guilty the first day. By Friday, the report was done, on time, and he'd gone to the gym twice. He noticed he was calmer in meetings.

qa.q: When was the report due?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he left early the first day?
qa.a: He felt guilty, still believing that staying late showed commitment.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that helped Hemant change?
qa.a: She shared her own burnout story and suggested a specific leaving time for the week.

qa.q: How might Hemant's girlfriend be affected by the change?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and closer to him if he has time for weekends again.

grounding: A young IT worker learns from his team lead to leave on time and avoid burnout.

passage:
Dear Jyoti,
You asked why I've stopped replying to work emails after eight. Here's the story.
For my first year in the firm, I answered everything, instantly, at midnight, on Sundays. I thought that was what a good employee did. I stopped seeing you. I stopped cycling. I snapped at Amma over nothing.
In March, I sat in the office bathroom and couldn't stop my hands shaking. That scared me.
I talked to my manager. I expected a lecture. She said, "Nobody asked you to answer at midnight." We agreed on a cut-off time. I also started seeing the company counsellor.
Now I cycle on Saturdays again. My work hasn't suffered. I just stopped suffering with it.
Come cycling this Saturday?
Tushar

qa.a: After eight.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel in the office bathroom in March?
qa.a: Tushar felt scared and overwhelmed, unable to stop the hands shaking.

qa.q: What steps helped Tushar set boundaries?
qa.a: Talking to the manager, agreeing on a cut-off time, and seeing the company counsellor.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jyoti may feel relieved and happy to have a friend back, and glad to be invited cycling.

passage:
Kashish, you want this for your podcast about first jobs? Fine. I'm Vijay, and my first job nearly flattened me.
In college, I had holidays, free afternoons, friends everywhere. Then I joined a consulting firm. Twelve-hour days. Weekend calls. I told myself it was just the first year.
By month eight I couldn't remember my last proper meal. I'd fall asleep with my laptop open.
One day my younger sister visited and said, "You don't laugh anymore." That hit harder than any review.
So I started small. Laptop closed at nine. Sunday mornings, no phone. I told my manager I'd be offline on Sundays unless there was a real emergency. He agreed, which shocked me.
I still work hard. But now I have a life to come home to.

qa.q: What did Vijay's younger sister say?
qa.a: "You don't laugh anymore."

qa.q: How did Vijay feel hearing that from the younger sister?
qa.a: Vijay felt hurt and shaken; it hit harder than any review.

qa.q: What boundaries did Vijay set, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Closing the laptop at nine and keeping Sunday mornings offline, which protect rest and relationships from burnout.

qa.q: How might the manager see Vijay's request?
qa.a: He agreed, so he may see it as reasonable and value Vijay staying healthy for the long run.

grounding: A young professional describes setting boundaries after the shift from student life to work.

passage:
I'm Ankita. I sit next to Harish at the software company. When we joined together last year, he was the first in and the last out, every day.
By December he looked grey. He'd eat lunch at his desk while fixing bugs. Once I saw him fall asleep in a meeting.
In January something changed. He started leaving at six. He put a little sign on his desk: "Back tomorrow at 9." He joined the Tuesday badminton group. I heard him tell our manager, very politely, that he couldn't take calls after eight except for emergencies.
I don't know what happened over the holidays. Maybe someone said something. Maybe he just got tired.
His work seems better, actually. Fewer mistakes. He laughs more.

qa.q: What did Harish's desk sign say?
qa.a: "Back tomorrow at 9."

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling by December?
qa.a: He was probably exhausted and burnt out, looking grey and falling asleep in a meeting.

qa.q: How could a team support someone setting boundaries like Harish?
qa.a: The team could respect his off hours, avoid late calls, and join him in activities like badminton.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Harish's change?
qa.a: Ankita notices his work and mood improved, though Ankita admits not knowing what caused the change.

grounding: A colleague observes a young professional setting boundaries to recover from burnout.

passage:
Monday, 12:40 a.m. Tejas was still answering emails on the sofa, laptop hot on his knees. His flatmate Vikas came out for water. "Weren't you going to sleep at eleven?" "One more," Tejas said. It was the ninth "one more". In college, late nights ended with the semester. Here, they just kept coming.
Thursday. He snapped at a teammate over nothing and sat in the bathroom stall for ten minutes, breathing. That evening he told Vikas, "I think I'm running on empty." They made a rule together: work notifications off at eight, laptop stays on the desk, not the sofa. Tejas told his lead he'd reply to non-urgent mails in the morning. She said, "Good. I should do that too."
The next Sunday, Tejas played cricket in the colony ground for the first time in two months. His phone stayed in his bag. He dropped two catches and laughed about both.

qa.a: He was on the sofa, with the laptop hot on his knees.

qa.q: How can you tell Tejas felt overwhelmed by Thursday?
qa.a: He snapped at a teammate over nothing and hid in the bathroom stall to breathe, then admitted he was running on empty, which shows he was exhausted and stressed. 😔

qa.q: What small steps helped Tejas set boundaries?
qa.a: Turning work notifications off at eight, keeping the laptop on the desk, and telling his lead he would answer non-urgent mail in the morning.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas to watch Tejas over these days?
qa.a: Vikas seems concerned at first, then relieved to help make a plan and see his flatmate relaxed enough to laugh at dropped catches.
